consensus_summary: All four blind responses agree that 'grafted in' refers to Paul's olive tree metaphor in Romans 11: Gentile believers (wild olive branches) are incorporated by faith into the covenant people of God rooted in Israel's patriarchal promises, with warnings against Gentile pride and the affirmation that broken-off natural branches (unbelieving Israel) can be grafted back in if they abandon unbelief.
book_summary: The book identifies grafting as the wild branch — the stranger, the Gentile — received into the covenant tree, or repentant Israel accepted back into it.
consensus_core_identification: Grafting = Gentile inclusion into God's covenant people/tree (Romans 11:17-24), coupled with the possibility of unbelieving Israel's regrafting upon repentance (Romans 11:23).
book_core_identification: Grafting = the Gentile stranger received into the covenant tree, or repentant Israel accepted back in.
boundary_disagreement: None of substance. The book's compact definition explicitly names both cases the consensus identifies: Gentile inclusion (Rom 11:17) and regrafting of repentant Israel (Rom 11:23). The consensus responses treat the regrafting as part of the same passage's teaching, so the book's disjunctive phrasing simply foregrounds what the consensus already contains.
material_contradiction: None. Both readings identify the same referent (incorporation into God's covenant people via Paul's olive tree image) covering the same two cases.
rationale: The book's entry is a condensed restatement of the consensus reading. It names the Gentile as the wild branch received into the covenant tree — exactly the consensus's primary meaning — and adds 'repentant Israel accepted back,' which corresponds directly to Romans 11:23, a verse every consensus response includes in its account of the metaphor (regrafting of natural branches). The book calls the tree the 'covenant tree,' consistent with the consensus's 'covenant people rooted in the patriarchs.' No boundary is moved, no case is excluded or reclassified, and no downstream dispute (supersessionism, dispensational tree-identity, individual soteriology) is invoked by the entry. Differences are wording and compression only.
strongest_objection: One could argue the book's 'or repentant Israel accepted back' makes regrafting a coordinate primary meaning rather than a subsidiary implication, slightly reweighting the emphasis relative to the consensus's Gentile-centered primary meaning; but since every consensus response includes Israel's regrafting within the same metaphor and passage, this is a difference of emphasis, not extension.
